newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Q1 ECI eases fears of ominous wage pressures.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Q1 ECI eases fears of ominous wage pressures.

text.p: A benign report on U.S. labor costs in the first quarter surprised credit markets, easing fears of wage pressures, analysts said.
The Labor Department reported the Employment Cost Index (ECI) rose 0.6 percent over the first three months of 1997, much lower than the 0.9 percent consensus forecast of economists polled by Reuters.

"The real surprise to me was the fact that benefits only increased one-tenth of a percent again in the first quarter of this year," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
As in previous ECI reports, benefits costs grew more slowly than wages and salaries. Some analysts had expected the growth rate of benefits costs to rebound.
Benefits costs rose a meager 0.1 percent in the first three months of 1997, sharply lower than the 0.7 percent rise in the fourth quarter of 1996.
Many analysts had expected to see acceleration in medical cost increases, but that did not materialize.

"It's at least three quarters in a row that we have gotten a surprise on the low side. Everyone is waiting for benefits to bottom out but we didn't get it this time," said Raphael Marrone, money market economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Meanwhile, wages and salaries rose 0.9 percent in the 1997 first quarter, slightly more than the 0.8-percent rise over the last three months in 1996.
But wage and salary components failed to post an increase of one percent or greater, and that offered some relief, said James Padinha, an economist at Briefing.Com.
"This starts the ball rolling in terms of maybe the (Federal Reserve) doesn't tighten," he said.
Some experts argued that the ECI report does not change the general concern at the Federal Reserve.

"It's good news, but I don't think it changes fear at the Fed that in time the tightness in the labor market will be reflected in rising employment costs and then in rising consumer prices," Liro said.

For now, however, investors embraced the ECI report and a market-friendly durable goods report that showed orders down 3.0 percent in March, below the consensus forecast of unchanged and far below February's revised 0.8-percent increase.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond surged over a full point before settling at 95.03 bid to yield 7.02 percent at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
"Two days from now we get a key NAPM report, and Friday we get employment, so the whole thing starts all over again," Padinha said.
